--- title: "Time Series Forecasting" description: "Chapter 16: dependence over time, trend, seasonality and noise, pandas datetime index, autocorrelation, STL decomposition, benchmarks, ETS and Fourier ARIMA, test periods, and prediction intervals." format: deck-html execute: echo: false freeze: auto --- # Time Series Forecasting When the order of observations carries information **Chapter 16** Polla Fattah --- ## By the end of today you can - explain dependence over time, and why forecasts are ranges; - name the parts of a series: trend, seasonality, noise; - store a series in pandas with a datetime index, and plot it; - read time plots, seasonal plots, and autocorrelation; - decompose a series with STL; - forecast with benchmarks, ETS, and ARIMA; - evaluate forecasts on a test period, and report prediction intervals. --- ## A different way of thinking | Survey data | Time series | |---|---| | observations independent | this week relates to last week | | order does not matter | order carries information | | one value per case | trend, season, and noise together | A forecast of the future is honestly a range, never a single number. --- ## The counselling service's question Five years of weekly visit counts: overwhelmed before exams, quiet in summer, staffing planned by guesswork. How many visits should the service expect next year, week by week? An **internal analysis**, done for the service rather than for publication. --- ## A pandas series knows which column is time ```python clinic = pd.DataFrame({ 'day': range(1, 15), 'visits': [12, 10, 9, 11, 7, 3, 2, 14, 11, 10, 12, 8, 4, 2] }).set_index('day') ``` Two weeks of daily visits to a small clinic, from a Monday. The **index** keeps observations in chronological order. Busy early in the week, quiet at the weekend. --- ## Three parts of a pattern ```python weeks = np.arange(1, 157) trend = 30 + 0.05 * weeks seasonal = 12 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * weeks / 52) noise = np.random.normal(0, 3, 156) series = trend + seasonal + noise ``` An artificial weekly series for three years, built from its parts. --- ## Only the sum is observed ::: {#49858056 .cell fig-height='4.3' fig-width='9' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=842 height=392} ::: ::: Forecasting extends trend and season. Noise cannot be forecast: the main reason every forecast has a range. --- ## The counselling data in pandas ```python counselling_visits = dt.load_counselling_visits() counselling_visits['week_start'] = pd.to_datetime(counselling_visits['week_start']) visits = counselling_visits.set_index('week_start').sort_index() ``` Five academic years, September 2020 to August 2025: 260 weeks. `week_start` as `DatetimeIndex` aligns each observation to regular weekly Monday intervals. --- ## Plot the series first ::: {#d8c75b2d .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='9' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=843 height=305} ::: ::: A seasonal pattern each academic year, a gentle upward trend, noise, and one unusual week in autumn 2023. --- ## A seasonal plot ::: {#b0e84ae0 .cell fig-height='3.5' fig-width='9' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=843 height=315} ::: ::: Every year has the same shape; later years lie slightly higher. The period is 52 weeks. --- ## Busy weeks follow busy weeks ::: {#6e8caabb .cell fig-height='3.9' fig-width='5.5' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=507 height=353} ::: ::: Knowing last week's visits says a good deal about this week's. --- ## Autocorrelation The correlation between the series and itself $k$ steps earlier. ```python visits_acf = acf(visits['visits'], nlags=60) ``` | Lag | 1 | 26 | 52 | |---|---|---|---| | autocorrelation | 0.69 | −0.24 | 0.68 | A week resembles the same week a year earlier. Half a year apart, a busy term week often meets a quiet summer week. --- ## The autocorrelation function ::: {#e2a7f8bc .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='9' execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=842 height=305} ::: ::: A peak at the seasonal lag is the signature of seasonality. No autocorrelation would mean nothing to forecast beyond the average. --- ## Decomposition with STL ```python stl = STL(visits['visits'], period=52, robust=True) visits_stl = stl.fit() ``` | Component | Is | |---|---| | trend | the slow movement | | seasonal | the repeating academic-year pattern | | remainder | what is left: the noise | `robust=True` stops unusual weeks from distorting trend and season. --- ## The recovered parts ::: {#69f9f050 .cell fig-height='4.3' fig-width='9' execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=842 height=392} ::: ::: The trend rises from about 35 to 41 visits a week, levelling off in the last year. --- ## The unusual week ```python decomp_df = pd.DataFrame({ 'week': visits.index, 'visits': visits['visits'], 'trend': visits_stl.trend, 'seasonal': visits_stl.seasonal, 'remainder': visits_stl.resid }) top_odd = decomp_df.iloc[decomp_df['remainder'].abs().argsort()[::-1][:1]] ``` The week of 23 October 2023: 71 visits, about 30 more than trend and season predict. It was the mental health awareness week. A real week, not an error: kept, and the robust fit stops it distorting forecasts. --- ## Growing seasonal swings The peaks get higher as the trend rises, while the summer lows stay low. When the season grows with the level, model the **logarithm** of the series: $$ \log(\text{visits}) = \text{trend} + \text{seasonal} + \text{noise} $$ Forecast on the log scale, then exponentiate back with `np.exp()`. --- ## Benchmarks first | Method | Forecasts | |---|---| | mean | the average of all past observations | | naive | the last observed value | | seasonal naive | the value from the same season last cycle | Every forecasting method must beat these, as every model in Chapters 11–13 had to beat a baseline. --- ## Benchmarks on the clinic ```python fc_mean = np.repeat(np.mean(clinic['visits']), 7) fc_naive = np.repeat(clinic['visits'].iloc[-1], 7) fc_snaive = clinic['visits'].iloc[-7:].values ``` | Method | Forecast for next week | |---|---| | mean | 8.4 every day | | naive | 2 every day: a quiet Sunday repeated | | seasonal naive | last week's pattern repeated | --- ## Two families of models | Family | Forecasts with | |---|---| | ETS (exponential smoothing) | weighted averages, recent weeks counting most; tracks level, trend, season | | ARIMA | how each value depends on earlier values and shocks | Both work best with short seasons: 4 quarters, 7 days, 12 months. A 52-week season is long. --- ## Two strategies for weekly data ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Weekly series"] --> B["STL: remove
the season"] --> C["ETS on the
adjusted series"] --> D["Add the
season back"] A --> E["ARIMA with
Fourier waves"] ``` Strategy 1: decompose with STL, fit ETS on adjusted data, add season back. Strategy 2: ARIMA with six pairs of harmonic waves. --- ## Training and test periods ```python train = visits[visits.index < '2024-09-01'] test = visits[visits.index >= '2024-09-01'] ``` The test period must come **after** the training period: a forecast can only use the past. Train on four academic years, test on the fifth. --- ## Five models compared ```python # STL + ETS stl_tr = STL(np.log(y_tr), period=52, robust=True).fit() sa_tr = np.log(y_tr) - stl_tr.seasonal ets_fit = Holt(sa_tr, initialization_method='estimated').fit() fc_stl_ets = np.exp(ets_fit.forecast(52) + stl_tr.seasonal[-52:]) ``` Fit benchmarks, STL + ETS, and Fourier ARIMA. --- ## Accuracy on the test year | Model | RMSE | MAE | |---|---|---| | STL + ETS | 9.3 | 6.8 | | Seasonal Naive | 9.2 | 7.0 | | Fourier ARIMA | 11.4 | 8.9 | | Mean | 18.7 | 16.3 | | Naive | 27.5 | 23.5 | STL with ETS is best. The Fourier model struggles with sharp steps, such as the sudden drop into summer. --- ## The two best, against reality ::: {#64e75a0e .cell fig-height='3.5' fig-width='9' execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=841 height=315} ::: ::: The seasonal naive copies last year's noise, even the awareness-week spike. STL with ETS is smoother and closer. --- ## Forecasting next year ```python stl_all = STL(np.log(y_all), period=52, robust=True).fit() sa_all = np.log(y_all) - stl_all.seasonal ets_all = Holt(sa_all, initialization_method='estimated').fit() fc_log_next = ets_all.forecast(52) + stl_all.seasonal[-52:] fc_next = np.exp(fc_log_next) ``` Refitted on all five years, so the forecasts use the most recent information. --- ## Prediction intervals ::: {#80c37e8a .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='9' execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](16-time-series_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=840 height=305} ::: ::: First week: about 24 visits, anywhere from 17 to 33 unsurprising. --- ## A total for the year needs simulation ```python np.random.seed(2026) resid = stl_all.resid futures = [] for _ in range(1000): sim_noise = np.random.choice(resid, size=52, replace=True) sim_path = np.exp(fc_log_next + sim_noise) futures.append(np.sum(sim_path)) q = np.quantile(futures, [0.025, 0.5, 0.975]).round() ``` Weeks do not vary independently, so weekly intervals cannot simply be added. Residual bootstrap simulation produces 1,000 possible futures; their totals give the range. --- ## The report to the service - about **2,177** visits expected in 2025/26 (95% interval 2,050 to 2,464), against 2,056 in 2024/25; - the busiest weeks will again be just before and during the exam periods; - an awareness campaign can raise demand sharply for a week: plan extra capacity. --- ## Forecasts assume the future resembles the past A new booking system, a changed exam calendar, or a crisis like COVID-19 can make any forecast wrong. - report forecasts with their intervals; - say what they assume; - update them as new data arrives. --- ## In your field: environmental science ```python co2_m = co2_raw['co2'].resample('MS').mean().ffill()['1959-01-01':'1997-12-01'] # Train through 1990, forecast 1991-1997 (7 years) ``` | Model | MAE (ppm) | |---|---| | Seasonal Naive | 5.1 | | ETS | 1.0 | | SARIMAX | 1.1 | Mauna Loa CO₂: a strong trend and a 12-month cycle that ETS and ARIMA model directly. --- ## Practical lab: the Chapter 16 playground Work through the playground exercises in your browser, with hints and solutions. Run interactive Python code with Pyodide; download the complete offline project. --- ## Practical exercises 1–4: parts and models 1. Which benchmark suits a trend without seasonality? Test it on the clinic. 2. Plot the seasonally adjusted series: what does it reveal? 3. Fourier terms with $K = 2$ and $K = 12$. 4. Train on three years, test on the fourth. --- ## Practical exercises 5–7: forecasts and communication 5. Expected visits in the four weeks before the first exams, with an interval. 6. Explain a 95% prediction interval to the service. 7. Double the noise in the artificial series: what happens to forecast intervals? --- ## Try this yourself Find a series in your own field. - plot it, and name its trend, season, and noise; - choose the seasonal period; - pick a benchmark it must beat; - decide what event could make a forecast wrong. --- ## Troubleshooting guide (Part 1) | Symptom | Likely cause | |---|---| | "duplicated index" error | the same timestamp appears twice | | ETS or ARIMA struggles with weekly data | the 52-week season is long; decompose first | | forecasts copy last year's spikes | seasonal naive repeats the noise | | one week dominates the trend | use `robust=True` | --- ## Troubleshooting guide (Part 2) | Symptom | Likely cause | |---|---| | test error suspiciously low | test period not after training period | | seasonal swings grow with the level | model `np.log()` of the series | | a yearly total without an interval | weekly intervals cannot be added; simulate | | forecasts wrong after a change | the past no longer resembles the future | --- ## Completion checklist - [ ] the series has a clean datetime index; - [ ] time, seasonal, and ACF plots were inspected; - [ ] the series was decomposed, and unusual weeks explained; - [ ] benchmarks are reported; - [ ] models are tested on a later period; - [ ] forecasts include prediction intervals; - [ ] totals come from simulation; - [ ] assumptions are stated. --- ## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 1) | Misconception | Better mental model | |---|---| | a forecast predicts the exact value | a forecast is a range | | more history always helps | only if old patterns still hold | --- ## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 2) | Misconception | Better mental model | |---|---| | any random subset can be the test set | the test period comes after training | | an unusual week should be removed | keep it; use robust methods | --- ## The chapter in one sentence > **Separate trend, season, and noise, beat the simple benchmarks on a later test period, and always report a forecast as a range with its assumptions.** --- ## Next: Chapter 17 The next chapter makes research reproducible: - reproducibility and credibility; - documents that contain their own analysis; - a results chapter in Quarto; - fixed package versions; - interactive dashboards and open science. --- ## Questions What regular measurement in your field has a seasonal pattern? What event could break its forecast?
